cover.headline: A strong domestic tyre brand caught in a raw-material squeeze, with a Camso bet still losing money: fairly priced after the sector de-rating
cover.lead: CEAT makes two-wheeler, car, truck, farm and off-highway tyres in six Indian plants and, since Sep-2025, Camso construction tyres and rubber tracks in Sri Lanka (bought from Michelin). Q1FY27 showed both sides of the story: standalone revenue +18.3% (volume +13-14%), but raw materials up 16-18% in a quarter cut the EBITDA margin to 8.5%, and a ₹48 cr Sri Lankan-rupee loss plus Camso start-up costs left consolidated profit at ₹4 cr. We forecast EPS of ₹114.0 / ₹236.0 / ₹278.0 for FY27-29E, close to Motilal Oswal. The street values CEAT on **P/E on one-year-forward EPS** (MOSL ~18x FY28E; Emkay 18x FY28E). The house rule (its forward P/E median since 2021, 16.6x, cut by the 21.9% tyre-sector de-rating) gives **13x Sep-28E EPS of ₹257.0 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD**. Cross-checks: DCF ₹4,441; EV/EBITDA ₹2,681. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: A domestic franchise that keeps growing
arguments.p: CEAT leads two-wheeler replacement (~31% share), is third in cars (~17%) and holds ~25% of OEM electric car and two-wheeler fitments. Standalone revenue grew 15.5% in FY26 and 18.3% in Q1FY27, with replacement up mid-teens, OEM low teens and exports ~30%. New car-tyre (Chennai) and two-wheeler (Nagpur, plus ₹1,205 cr approved in July) capacity supports it. We model standalone revenue +14.8% / +10.8% / +10.1% for FY27-29E.

arguments.h: The margin squeeze is a lag, but a deep one
arguments.p: Gross margin fell to 33.5% in Q1 against the 40-41% management calls normal; Q2 adds another 8-10% of raw-material inflation. CEAT had taken ~11% of the ~15-16% price increase it needs by mid-July, with OEM index increases from 1-Jul. We assume a standalone margin of 10.7% for FY27E and 13% by FY29E, below FY26's 13.4%.

CEAT paid ₹1,186 cr for Camso and owes ~₹420 cr (USD44 mn) more for the brand in 2028. Until customers move from Michelin (90% by Sep-2026) and the plant gets its own mixers (by Mar-2027), CEAT sells through Michelin at 25-30% less and Camso loses money at EBITDA. We assume a 0% margin in FY27E, 8% in FY28E and 10% in FY29E on ₹1,200-1,330 cr of revenue.

At ₹3,264 CEAT trades at 13.8x our FY28E and 12.7x Sep-28E EPS, against a 16.6x forward median since 2021. Tyre stocks were 21.9% below their five-year medians on 30-Sep-2026 (MRF and Apollo much more), so 13x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}, below the post-Q1 street median (₹4,266), which applies 16-18x without that de-rating. The stock is 21% below its Oct-2025 high.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (typically mid-October): the size of the second raw-material step-up (8-10% q/q) against ~15% of replacement price increases and the OEM index increase from 1-Jul.
Natural rubber after the monsoon: domestic ~₹280/kg in July (a 15-year high, ₹15-20 above import parity); management expects it to follow crude down once the West Asia conflict eases.
Camso in H2FY27: the first quarters with ~90% of customers billed directly; whether the business turns EBITDA positive.
The Sri Lankan rupee: USD24.5 mn of the USD80 mn intra-group loan converts to equity; further LKR falls still hit finance cost.
Capacity: Chennai car tyres to 130 lakh a year by FY28, Nagpur two-wheeler to 100,000 a day, and the ₹1,205 cr two-wheeler project.

sections.title: A brand-led Indian tyre maker, strongest in two-wheelers, with a new global off-highway niche

blocks.p: CEAT sells tyres for trucks and buses (29% of FY26 standalone revenue), two- and three-wheelers (27%), passenger cars and UVs (22%), off-highway vehicles such as tractors and construction machines (15%) and light commercial vehicles (7%). By channel, 51% went to the replacement market through dealers, 30% to vehicle makers (OEMs) and 19% abroad (FY25: 53% / 28% / 19%). MOSL puts CEAT at ~31% of two-wheeler replacement (the leader), ~17% of cars (third) and ~10% of truck radials. It made 4.5 crore tyres in FY26 in six Indian plants (Bhandup, Nashik, Halol, Nagpur, Chennai, Ambernath) at more than 80% utilisation, 85-90% by Q4FY26.

Since 1-Sep-2025 CEAT also owns the Camso brand's construction-equipment bias tyres and rubber tracks business, bought from Michelin with a plant in Sri Lanka (~220 tonnes a day). It added ₹421 cr of revenue in seven months of FY26 and takes international revenue to ~23% of the group (20% standalone). The Sri Lankan joint venture CEAT Kelani (tyres for Sri Lanka) is equity-accounted (₹16 cr of profit share in FY26).

sections.title: From a Mumbai tyre plant to six Indian factories and a Sri Lankan off-highway business

blocks.p: CEAT Tyres of India was set up in 1958 (with the Tatas) and has been part of the RPG group since 1982; the Goenka family controls it through holding companies (47.3%). The last decade was about building capacity in the consumer-facing categories (two-wheeler radials at Nagpur, car radials at Chennai, off-highway tyres at Ambernath) and, in FY26, buying a global off-highway brand. Profit has followed the raw-material cycle more than any corporate action.

sections.title: Indian tyres: GST-led demand in FY26, a raw-material squeeze in FY27 and a capex wave

blocks.p: Indian tyre industry revenue ~₹1.36 lakh cr in FY26; the top six makers are ~85% of it (CRISIL, 24-Aug-2026). Demand follows the vehicle parc, freight and farm incomes (replacement), new vehicle sales (OEM) and exports. CRISIL (24-Aug-2026): volume growth slows to 4-5% in FY27 after 7-8% in FY26; key inputs up 35-40%; natural rubber ~₹275/kg in Jun-2026 vs ~₹220/kg in FY26; operating margin down 200-250 bp to ~11.5-12% in FY27 (from ~14.2%), recovering to 13-13.5% in FY28 if input costs stabilise; "a cost-pass-through lag rather than a structural profitability reset"; the top six plan ~₹18,000 cr of capex over FY27-28, nearly double the previous two years.

bullets: **Demand.** GST on most tyres cut from 28% to 18% in Sep-2025 (farm tyres 18% to 5%) and lower GST on vehicles lifted replacement and OEM demand in H2FY26; CEAT expects mid-single-digit replacement growth in truck and car tyres and high single digits in two-wheelers, with El Nino and the West Asia conflict as risks (Q1FY27 call).

**Raw materials.** Kottayam RSS-4 ₹273/kg on 3-Sep-2026; global futures near the highest since 2013 (Procurement Resource, 10-Sep-2026). CEAT (17-Jul-2026): domestic ~₹280/kg, a ₹15-20 premium to import parity; SICOM $2,180-2,200/t; two-thirds of its natural rubber is imported. Rubber (natural and synthetic) was ₹4,911 cr of CEAT's ₹9,508 cr raw-material bill in FY26; carbon black ₹1,435 cr, fabrics ₹756 cr.

**Pricing.** Industry took 7-9% of price increases by Q1FY27 with more planned in Q2 (CLSA via Moneycontrol, 12-Aug-2026); CEAT ~11% in replacement by mid-July and 4-6% more planned; MRF and others raised prices "in different measures, in different categories" (CEAT MD, 17-Jul-2026).

**Off-highway.** Off-highway construction tyres and tracks (Camso): a global niche led by Michelin/Camso, Bridgestone and others; US tariff 10% on Sri Lankan OHT tyres and tracks, 25% on the steel in tracks (Q1FY27 call).

**Regulation and imports.** DGFT licensing of tyre imports since Jun-2020 limits Chinese imports; EPR for waste tyres; four Labour Codes effective 21-Nov-2025 (CEAT booked ₹58 cr of past-service cost).

**Competition.** MRF, Apollo, CEAT and JK Tyre lead in India; MRF is the largest and the price leader; BKT dominates farm and off-highway exports; Chinese imports are limited by licensing. CEAT is strongest where the brand matters most to the buyer (two-wheelers, cars) and weakest in truck radials.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the demand tailwind reaches CEAT more than most peers because its mix is tilted to two-wheelers and cars, where the GST cut and premiumisation help most. What it cannot escape is the raw-material cycle, and Camso adds a second, company-specific source of noise for at least another year.

sections.title: The core: volume growth is strong; the margin is hostage to rubber and to how fast prices move

blocks.p: The standalone company (all six Indian plants, domestic and export sales) was ₹15,215 cr of FY26 revenue (+15.5%) with a 13.4% EBITDA margin and ₹812 cr of profit. In Q1FY27 revenue rose 18.3% (two-thirds volume, one-third price and mix): replacement up mid-teens, OEM low teens and international ~30%. But raw materials rose 16-18% over Q4 (domestic natural rubber ~₹280/kg, crude above $100, the rupee from 93-94 to 96.5) and the gross margin fell to 33.5%, so EBITDA fell to ₹380 cr (9.1%). Management expects another 8-10% of cost inflation in Q2.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** CEAT's volumes are strong and its brand lets it push prices, but the gap is unusually large: ~15-16% of increases needed in four months. We assume the standalone margin recovers to ~13% in H2 and to 12.8% in FY28E, still below FY26's 13.4%, because the whole industry is adding capacity. If rubber falls while prices hold (as management intends), FY28 margins could be higher; that is our bull case.

sections.title: Camso: a global brand bought at ~1x revenue, losing money until the Michelin transition ends

blocks.p: Camso makes bias tyres and rubber tracks for compact construction equipment (skid-steer loaders, mini-excavators) under the Camso and Hauler brands, in Sri Lanka. CEAT signed for it on 6-Dec-2024 and closed on 1-Sep-2025, paying ₹1,186 cr; the brand itself (USD44 mn) transfers after three years. During the transition CEAT sells to Michelin, which resells to customers and keeps 25-30% of the value chain, and the plant buys compounds from Michelin because it has no mixers or calenders. Customer prices run at ~USD10 mn a month (~USD120 mn a year); 60% of customers had moved to CEAT by June and 90% were expected by September; the upstream equipment (USD30 mn) is due by Q4FY27, so FY28 is the first year CEAT controls the whole chain.

So far the numbers are poor. Subsidiary revenue (consolidated less standalone) was ₹155 cr in Q1FY27, down 15% q/q, and EBITDA about −₹15 cr as CEAT opened warehouses and offices in Germany, the UK, France, Poland and the US before the revenue moved over. Q1 also carried a ₹48 cr finance-cost hit because the Sri Lankan Camso entity owes the parent USD80 mn and the Sri Lankan rupee fell from ~315 to ~335 per dollar; it cannot be hedged. USD24.5 mn of that loan is being converted into equity. US tariffs are 10% on Sri Lankan OHT tyres and tracks (tracks ~50% of US sales) plus 25% on the steel in tracks.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** strategically sensible (a global brand in a niche CEAT already knew from Ambernath, bought for ~1x revenue with almost no goodwill), but the payback is slow. Even at our FY29E (₹133 cr of EBITDA) EBITDA is only ~8% of the ~₹1,600 cr outlay including the brand, before depreciation and tax: well below CEAT's cost of capital. Management talked about 12-13% margins on ₹1,000-1,200 cr of revenue; we will believe it when the H2FY27 numbers show direct billing working.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard
blocks.source: GAM research compilation (annual report, presentations and calls to Jul-2026; MOSL market shares)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** CEAT has a narrow moat in branded two-wheeler and car tyres: dealers and riders ask for it, it can raise prices first in those categories, and it wins OEM EV fitments. It has no moat against the raw-material cycle (nobody in Indian tyres does), it is sub-scale in truck radials, and Camso is a bet, not an advantage yet. Returns above the cost of capital come only in good years (ROE 15-17% in FY24 and FY26, 2-6% in FY22-23).

sections.title: Revenue up 131% in six years; profit has swung with rubber and crude

blocks.p: CEAT's revenue was ₹6,779 cr in FY20 and ₹15,678 cr in FY26 (15.0% a year): volume growth in two-wheeler, car and export tyres, price increases after the FY22-23 cost spike, and, in FY26, seven months of Camso (₹421 cr). Profit has been far more volatile. The EBITDA margin swung between 7.7% and 13.8% since FY18 because raw materials are ~60% of revenue (natural and synthetic rubber alone ~31% in FY26) and price increases follow costs with a lag. EPS went from ₹107 in FY21 to ₹18 in FY22, back to ₹159 in FY24 and ₹173 in FY26. Exceptional items are small (₹71 cr in FY26 for the new labour codes and VRS), so reported and adjusted EPS tell the same story (MOSL adjusted FY26 EPS ₹185.1).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** CEAT is a well-run, brand-led tyre maker in a commodity-cost business. In good years (FY24, FY26) it earns 13-14% EBITDA margins and ROE of 15-17%; in bad years (FY22-23) margins fall to 8% and ROE to 2-6%. FY27 has started as a bad year: raw materials up 16-18% in one quarter cut the Q1 margin to 8.5%. Anyone buying CEAT is buying the cycle and the management's ability to push prices through.

bullets: **Demand:** replacement mid-teens, OEM low teens, international ~30%; standalone volume +13-14%. Management expects mid-single-digit replacement growth for truck and car tyres and high single digits for two-wheelers, double-digit OEM car and two-wheeler demand; "some moderation" in Q2 but "not going to fall off the cliff".

**Costs and prices:** raw materials +16-18% q/q in Q1 and +8-10% expected in Q2; ~11% of replacement price increases by mid-July with 4-6% more planned; OEM double-digit index increase from 1-Jul. If raw materials fall, CEAT intends to hold prices until the gross margin is back at 40-41%.
**Camso:** EBITDA negative in Q1 (start-up costs), ~60% of customers moved by June, ~90% by September; upstream by Q4FY27; FY28 the first full year of control.

**Finance cost and debt:** ₹146 cr incl. a ₹48 cr Sri Lankan-rupee loss; underlying ~₹98 cr, guided ~5% higher for the next one or two quarters. Debt ₹3,243 cr (₹3,011 cr at Mar-26), D/E 0.65x, debt/EBITDA 1.58x; working capital +₹138 cr (more raw-material stock, GST credits).
**Capex:** ₹293 cr in Q1; FY27 guidance 1,300-1,400 (India) cr; ₹1,205 cr approved for 53,000 more two-wheeler tyres a day by FY31. Credit rating: India Ratings AA (Positive) / A1+ reaffirmed.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** Q1 was the bottom of the margin cycle on management's own description, and two items made profit look worse than operations: the ₹48 cr currency loss and Camso's start-up costs. Even so, Q2 will be weak (more cost inflation, the OEM increase arriving only in July). Our FY27E EBITDA margin of {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} assumes ~9% standalone in Q2, ~11.5% in Q3 and ~13% in Q4.

sections.title: Heavy capex every year, an acquisition in FY26 and returns that only beat the cost of capital in good years

blocks.p: CEAT has built capacity almost every year: ₹3,348 cr of capex in FY18-21 (Nagpur, Chennai, Ambernath) and ₹4,795 cr in FY22-26 against ₹6,421 cr of operating cash. On top came the Camso purchase: ₹1,186 cr paid on 1-Sep-2025, with ~₹420 cr (USD44 mn) more due for the Camso brand three years after closing and ~USD44 mn of finished goods to buy from Michelin over 12 months. Borrowings (incl. leases) rose from ₹2,136 cr to ₹3,272 cr in FY26. ROCE (Screener) was 14%, 6%, 9%, 20%, 15%, 19% in FY21-26: below a ~12% cost of capital in FY22-23, above it in the good years. The next leg is already approved: ₹1,300-1,400 cr of India capex in FY27 (car tyres at Chennai, two-wheelers at Nagpur), USD20-25 mn for Camso's upstream mixers and calenders, and a further ₹1,205 cr for 53,000 two-wheeler tyres a day by FY31.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** CEAT keeps reinvesting at ~8% of revenue and has now added a ₹1,600 cr acquisition (incl. the brand) that has not yet made money. Returns are fine at the top of the cycle (ROE 16% in FY26) and poor at the bottom. We model ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}} / {{F.roe.1|pct}} / {{F.roe.2|pct}} for FY27-29E and thin free cash flow until FY28E.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean accounts and good cash conversion; currency and acquisition noise in FY26-27

bullets: **Cash conversion is strong.** Cash from operations was ₹1,786 cr in FY26 against EBITDA of ₹2,064 cr (87%), helped by supplier credit and dealer deposits (negative working capital). It dipped to ₹1,092 cr in FY25 when receivables and inventories rose.

**Exceptional items are small but recurring.** ₹71 cr in FY26 (labour codes ₹58 cr, VRS ₹13 cr), ₹30 cr in FY25, ₹58 cr in FY24, ₹7 cr in Q1FY27 (VRS). Screener nets them into other income. Reported FY26 EPS ₹172.8 vs MOSL adjusted ₹185.1: a 7% gap.

**Acquisition accounting.** Camso's ₹1,186 cr was allocated mostly to plant (₹763 cr) and know-how and licences (₹311 cr, amortised), with only ₹7.2 cr of goodwill (independent valuer; key audit matter). ₹23.4 cr of deal costs went through other expenses in FY26. The USD44 mn brand payment is a disclosed commitment, not a liability.
**Currency in finance cost.** The ₹48 cr Sri Lankan-rupee loss in Q1FY27 sits in finance cost, not in exceptional items; it can reverse if the rupee recovers. We assume no further loss.

**Other income is small.** FY26 ₹40.4 cr (interest ₹7.7 cr, FX gains ₹22.1 cr, other ₹10.6 cr) plus the JV share ₹15.8 cr. We forecast ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.1|num}} / {{F.otherIncome.2|num}} cr including the JV.
**Tax.** The consolidated rate (28.6% in FY26, 103% in Q1FY27) is above the standalone ~25% because Camso and Sri Lankan losses get no tax credit.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Clean audit (B S R & Co.), small exceptional items, strong cash conversion and full standalone/consolidated disclosure every quarter. Watch the Camso amortisation, the brand commitment and the Sri Lankan currency line.

sections.title: Net debt of ₹2,967 cr at Mar-26 (₹3,243 cr of debt at Jun-26): comfortable, but rising

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 CEAT had ₹3,011 cr of borrowings (₹1,504 cr long-term) and ~₹260 cr of lease liabilities against just ₹43 cr of cash: net debt of ₹2,967 cr before leases, 1.46x EBITDA and 0.6x equity (company). Debt rose to ₹3,243 cr at Jun-26 (1.58x LTM EBITDA) on capex and ₹138 cr more working capital. CEAT runs on supplier and dealer money: payables of ~132 days and ₹645 cr of dealer deposits fund ~68 days of inventory and ~43 of receivables (Screener), so working capital is negative. Off the balance sheet: ₹1,785 cr of capital commitments (₹706 cr a year earlier), the USD44 mn Camso brand payment and ₹275 cr of contingent liabilities (mostly GST and excise disputes). India Ratings reaffirmed AA (Positive) in Q1FY27.

sections.title: The street after Q1: mostly Buy, targets ₹4,015-4,500, median ₹4,266

blocks.p: After the Q1FY27 results (16-17 Jul-2026) Motilal Oswal kept Buy with ₹4,228 (~18x FY28E EPS of ₹234.9), cutting FY27E EPS by 22% for the interest hit but leaving FY28E unchanged; Emkay kept Buy at ₹4,500 (18x FY28E in its 6-Jul sector note, which upgraded CEAT from Reduce; rolled to a Jun-27 target on 18-Jul), arguing margins have bottomed; ICICI Securities had Buy at ₹4,300 (20-Jul); Nomura Buy at ₹4,266 (20-Jul, from ₹4,276); Nirmal Bang moved to Hold at ₹4,015 (July). Median of the five post-Q1 targets: ₹4,266, +31% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹3,264. Before Q1, Nuvama (Hold, ₹3,900 at 16x FY28E), JM Financial (Add, ₹4,090) and Anand Rathi (Hold, ₹3,850) were more cautious. Everyone who discloses a method uses **P/E on one-year-forward EPS**; none we read used EV/EBITDA or a sum of the parts on or before 30-Sep-2026.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good brand at a cyclical low, priced about right; HOLD

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's two-wheeler tyre leader and a strong car-tyre brand, growing volume at double digits, with ~20% of revenue from exports and a newly bought global off-highway niche (Camso). Earnings are at a cyclical low: raw materials rose ~25% in two quarters and price increases lag; Camso is loss-making until FY28; a currency loss hit Q1. Debt is up to ₹3,243 cr after the acquisition and capex continues at ~8% of revenue.

**What you are paying:** 28.6x our FY27E and 13.8x FY28E EPS. CEAT's own forward P/E has a median of 16.6x since 2021; Indian tyre stocks were 21.9% below their five-year medians on 30-Sep-2026, which gives 13x Sep-28E EPS and {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): HOLD on our rule. The DCF (₹4,441) is above, EV/EBITDA (₹2,681) below.

bullets: **Rating: HOLD, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.

**We would turn BUY below ~₹2,905** and SELL above ~₹3,515 on today's numbers; we would raise the target if Q2-Q3FY27 show the gross margin recovering towards 38-40% and Camso breaking even, and cut it if margins stay near 9% into Q3.

**This is mainly a multiple call.** Our FY28E EPS (₹236.0) is close to MOSL's; our 13x sits below the street's 16-18x because tyre stocks have de-rated. At 16x our target would be ~₹4,110; the post-Q1 street median is ₹4,266.
**Biggest swing factor:** the margin. Each 1pp of EBITDA margin is ~₹37.4 of FY28E EPS; each 1x of multiple is ~₹257 a share.
